hero.title: Mitsubishi 4J10 Engine - Replacement Cost, Problems & Compatibility
hero.description: The 4J10 is Mitsubishi's 1.8‑litre SOHC MIVEC four‑cylinder petrol engine, introduced in 2011 as a more fuel‑efficient successor to the 4B10. Fitted to the ASX and Lancer from 2012 onward, it produces 139 hp and features next‑generation MIVEC technology that continuously regulates intake valve lift, duration and timing. Reconditioned 4J10 units typically start from £1,200+ supply‑only.

compatibility.title: Which Mitsubishi Models Use the 4J10?
compatibility.intro: The 4J10 was introduced in 2011 as Mitsubishi's next‑generation 1.8‑litre MIVEC engine. It debuted in the Japanese market RVR (ASX), Galant Fortis (Lancer) and Galant Fortis Sportback (Lancer Sportback), and was subsequently offered in UK‑spec ASX and Lancer models from 2012 onward.

costGuide.title: Mitsubishi 4J10 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a 4J10 typically takes 8-10 hours at £60-£70/hr (independent Mitsubishi specialist) - main dealer rates are significantly higher.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the service history - particularly whether the timing chain has been replaced and whether the engine has a history of oil consumption. A used unit with documented chain replacement and regular oil changes will command a premium. The 4J10 is a relatively straightforward engine to work on, but the MIVEC system is sensitive to oil quality, so a reconditioned unit with fresh oil seals and a new chain is often the better long‑term investment. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide for more detail.

failures.title: Mitsubishi 4J10 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Oil Consumption - MIVEC system sensitivity and piston ring wear
items.whatHappens: The 4J10's advanced MIVEC system is sensitive to oil quality, and owners have reported higher‑than‑normal oil consumption as mileage accumulates. The MIVEC and VVL systems are demanding on the quality of the oil used. If the wrong oil is used or oil changes are neglected, the variable valve lift system can become compromised, leading to increased wear on the piston rings and valve seals.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, switching to the correct 5W‑20 or 5W‑30 oil and more frequent changes can reduce consumption. If consumption is severe, piston ring replacement is possible (£800-£1,500) but is labour‑intensive. If oil consumption leads to carbon buildup or catalytic converter damage, a full engine replacement may be more cost‑effective. Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch - rattling noise on startup
items.whatHappens: The 4J10 uses a timing chain rather than a belt. However, as with many chain‑driven engines, the timing chain can stretch over time, particularly if oil changes have been neglected. Owners report a rattling noise on cold starts that may disappear as the engine warms up. If ignored, chain stretch can lead to timing errors, ECU fault codes, and eventually engine damage.
items.repairVsReplace: Timing chain replacement is a significant job (£500-£1,200) and should be undertaken promptly if rattling is heard. If the chain jumps or breaks, the interference engine design means pistons can hit valves - full engine replacement is the only option. Read our full timing chain failure guide

items.title: Ignition Coil Failure - misfires, rough idle, and Check Engine Light
items.whatHappens: Ignition coil failure is a common issue on the 4J10, leading to misfires, poor performance, rough idle, and the Check Engine Light illuminating. This is a well‑known issue on Mitsubishi engines of this era, and the 4J10 is no exception.
items.repairVsReplace: Ignition coil replacement is straightforward (£100-£300 per coil, or £200-£500 for a full set). Replacing spark plugs simultaneously is recommended (£40-£80).

items.title: Engine Vibration - worn engine mounts
items.whatHappens: Some owners report excessive engine vibration, which is often caused by worn engine mounts. The 4J10 is designed to be smooth, but ageing mounts can transmit vibration into the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: Engine mount replacement (£200-£500) typically resolves the issue and restores smoothness.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 4J10
variants.intro: The 4J10 is one of several 1.8‑litre engines in Mitsubishi's lineup. It is commonly confused with: | Similar Code | What It Is | Link | |---|---|---| | 4B10 | Previous‑generation 1.8L DOHC MIVEC (2005-2012) - fitted to earlier Lancers and ASX; uses DOHC rather than SOHC; different MIVEC system that only varies timing, not lift and duration | Mitsubishi 4B10 engine | | 4B11 | 2.0L DOHC MIVEC - larger displacement variant, fitted to Lancer 2.0 and some ASX models | Mitsubishi 4B11 engine | | 4J11 | 2.0L SOHC MIVEC - larger displacement variant of the 4J family | Mitsubishi 4J11 engine | How to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the cylinder block (typically on the front or side of the engine) and appears on the V5C registration document and in the vehicle's VIN. If you're unsure, enter your registration above - we'll confirm your exact fitment. Why the difference matters: The 4J10 is a fundamentally different engine from the 4B10 - it uses SOHC instead of DOHC, and its next‑generation MIVEC system continuously regulates intake valve lift, opening duration and timing simultaneously. Fitting a 4B10 into a 4J10‑spec vehicle is not a straight swap; ECU calibration, engine mounts, and emissions hardware differ.

relatives.description: - the older 1.8L DOHC MIVEC engine (2005-2012) that the 4J10 replaced; it uses a DOHC design with a different MIVEC system that only varies valve timing, not lift and duration simultaneously. The 4B10 is generally considered less advanced but simpler than the 4J10. If your car is pre‑2012, this is likely the engine you have.

- the 2.0L SOHC MIVEC sibling (2013+), producing around 150 hp and sharing the same 4J family architecture. It's a larger displacement variant with different bore/stroke and ECU calibration. If you're considering an upgrade for an ASX, this offers more power but is not a direct fit for 4J10 applications.

- the 2.0L DOHC MIVEC (2005-2015) fitted to Lancer 2.0 and some ASX models; it's from the older 4B family and features a different architecture (DOHC vs SOHC). It is not interchangeable with the 4J10.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 4J10 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used 4J10 can seem tempting at £600-£1,200, but carries significant risk. You don't know the condition of the timing chain, oil consumption history, or ignition coils - all of which can fail on higher‑mileage units. A used 4J10 with 60,000+ miles and no documented service history is a gamble. If you must buy used, insist on documented proof of regular oil changes using the correct 5W‑20 or 5W‑30 oil, and ideally a recent timing chain inspection.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** For most 4J10 replacements, a professionally reconditioned unit is the right call. A proper recon addresses the engine's known weak points: the timing chain and tensioner are replaced, piston rings are renewed (addressing oil consumption), ignition coils are tested or replaced, the water pump is replaced, and all gaskets and seals are renewed. With a 12‑24 month warranty, this is the lowest‑risk option for a £1,200-£2,500+ investment.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified for this engine only when the original block is in good condition and the vehicle has significant sentimental value - or if a specialist has confirmed that the engine can be saved with new internals. Expect £2,000-£3,500+ for a full rebuild. For most owners, a reconditioned exchange unit offers better value and less downtime.

items.question: How much does a Mitsubishi 4J10 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned 4J10 costs £1,200-£2,500+ supply‑only, plus £480-£700 for fitting at a specialist Mitsubishi workshop. Used units start from £600, and full rebuilds range from £2,000-£3,500+. Prices vary significantly by whether the timing chain, piston rings, and MIVEC components have been replaced. A used engine without documented oil change history using the correct 5W‑20/5W‑30 oil is a gamble - avoid it. Reconditioned units with new timing chain and piston rings command a premium.

items.question: What are the common problems with the 4J10?
items.answer: The most significant issues are oil consumption (caused by MIVEC system sensitivity and piston ring wear on higher‑mileage engines), timing chain stretch (causing rattling on startup), and ignition coil failure (causing misfires and Check Engine Light). The MIVEC system is demanding on oil quality - using the wrong oil can lead to premature wear. Regular oil changes (every 8,000-10,000 miles) using the correct 5W‑20 or 5W‑30 oil are critical. Listen for timing chain rattle on cold starts - replace promptly if heard.

items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt 4J10?
items.answer: For most owners, a reconditioned unit offers the best balance - it includes new timing chain, piston rings, ignition coils, water pump, and a 12‑24 month warranty. Used units are cheaper but carry risk of oil consumption and timing chain issues; full rebuilds are justified only if the original block is salvageable. Reconditioned from £1,200; used from £600; rebuilt from £2,000. A used engine without documented oil change history is a significant risk.

items.question: How do I tell the 4J10 apart from the 4B10?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the cylinder block (typically on the front or side of the engine), and appears on the V5C and in the VIN. The 4J10 is the SOHC MIVEC 1.8L from 2011 onward with next‑generation MIVEC (continuous valve lift, duration and timing). The 4B10 is the older DOHC MIVEC 1.8L (2005-2012) that only varies valve timing. The 4J10 uses a simpler SOHC design with more advanced MIVEC control. Fitting the wrong engine variant can cause ECU and emissions compatibility issues.
bullets: The 4J10 uses a simpler SOHC design with more advanced MIVEC control.
Fitting the wrong engine variant can cause ECU and emissions compatibility issues.

items.question: How reliable is the 4J10 compared to the older 4B10?
items.answer: The 4J10 is generally reliable when properly maintained, but is more sensitive to oil quality than the 4B10. The next‑generation MIVEC system demands regular oil changes using the correct 5W‑20 or 5W‑30 oil. The 4J10 is more fuel‑efficient and lighter than the 4B10, with less internal friction. However, the MIVEC system can become compromised if oil changes are neglected. Regular servicing and using the correct oil are critical to longevity. Many specialists recommend proactive timing chain replacement at 80,000-100,000 miles.
